definitionUse.use: Right circular cone; its axis is perpendicular to the circular base.
Surface versus solid is distinguished for rotation questions.
Cone lateral surface is a sector; lateral area pi*r*l.
Cone total surface adds exactly one base disk.
Frustum comes from parallel similar cone sections; radii and extended slants have the same ratio.
Rotation of trapezoid boundary includes the two end disks; rotating only two triangle legs produces two lateral cone surfaces, not an added internal disk.
Frustum net separates the annular-sector lateral band from the two base disks.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For a nondegenerate right circular cone: (1) an axial section is an isosceles triangle with equal slants and base a diameter; (2) an interior plane parallel to the base gives a disk (called a circle in the school section convention); (3) a cutting plane through the apex gives an isosceles triangle because both end-to-apex generators have the same length. The wording 'through the apex' alone also permits a supporting plane with only one generator as the intersection, or an exterior-to-the-cone plane with only the apex. A base-parallel plane at the apex gives a point. Thus the usual triangle/circle statements require genuine nondegenerate cuts; do not silently turn 'every plane through the apex' into 'every triangle'.
source_reviews.conditions: Positive radius and height; genuine cuts for the familiar shapes. Drawing/proof recognition loses independent construction but is not inherently a failed mathematical task.

source_reviews.independent_solution: No central symmetry: the unique apex would have to map to itself, forcing the center to be the apex, but reflecting any base point through it leaves the solid. Exactly one spatial symmetry/rotation axis, the apex-to-base-center line; infinitely many symmetry planes, precisely all planes through this line. A horizontal plane swaps an apex and a disk and is not a symmetry plane. Neither a generator nor a base diameter is a spatial symmetry axis.
source_reviews.conditions: Finite nondegenerate right circular cone, not a double cone. Spatial axis symmetry is not the count of symmetry axes of the base circle.

source_reviews.independent_solution: (1) Half the axial section is a right triangle, r=l*sin(phi/2), h=l*cos(phi/2), so base area is pi*l^2*sin(phi/2)^2. (2) r=sqrt(Q/pi), h=sqrt(l^2-Q/pi), and axial triangle area is (2r)*h/2 = sqrt((Q/pi)*(l^2-Q/pi)).
source_reviews.conditions: l>0, 0<phi<pi; for (2), 0<Q<pi*l^2. Boundary values describe degenerate solids, not ordinary cones.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Let apex S project to base center O, and let M be the foot from O on the trace chord line AB. h=R*tan(alpha). The angle between section and base is phi, so OM=d=h*cot(phi), SM=h/sin(phi), and half chord AM=sqrt(R^2-d^2). The triangular section area is AM*SM = R^2*tan(alpha)*sqrt(1-tan(alpha)^2*cot(phi)^2)/sin(phi). Equivalent form h*sqrt(R^2-h^2*cot(phi)^2)/sin(phi). At phi=pi/2 the section is axial and area is R*h. At phi=alpha it is tangent/one generator and area 0. For 0<phi<alpha no positive-area cut exists. This is a plane/base dihedral angle, not the angle between two generators.
source_reviews.conditions: R>0, 0<alpha<pi/2; nondegenerate triangular section alpha<phi<=pi/2. Tangency phi=alpha must not be claimed to produce a nondegenerate triangle.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Radius 3 m, height 2 m, slant sqrt(13) m; roof lateral area 3*pi*sqrt(13)=33.9815201974 m^2. Waste/joints are 10% OF ROOF AREA, so buy 1.1 times this, not divide by 0.9. Each sheet has area 0.7*1.4=0.98 m^2. Required count ceil(1.1*3*pi*sqrt(13)/0.98)=ceil(38.14252267057)=39 sheets. Roof excludes the base disk.
source_reviews.conditions: Whole sheets require upward rounding; m^2 cancels before rounding.

source_reviews.independent_solution: (1) The side opposite 30 degrees is the SHORT leg a, so the other leg is a*sqrt(3) and hypotenuse 2a. Altitude to rotation axis is common radius r=(a*a*sqrt(3))/(2a)=a*sqrt(3)/2. The two legs generate two cone lateral surfaces: pi*r*(a+a*sqrt(3)) = pi*a^2*(3+sqrt(3))/2. No disk is generated by this polyline and the common circle is an internal joining boundary. (2) With half-angle t=phi/2, equal side l=b/(2*sin(t)), altitude/common radius r=b/(2*tan(t)). Two lateral areas total 2*pi*r*l = pi*b^2*cos(t)/(2*sin(t)^2).
source_reviews.conditions: a,b>0 and 0<phi<pi. Rotate the stated two-segment boundary, not an arbitrary complete solid boundary.

source_reviews.independent_solution: The two generators both have length l and included angle alpha; section area S=l^2*sin(alpha)/2, hence l=sqrt(2S/sin(alpha)). Base radius r=sqrt(Q/pi). Lateral area pi*r*l=sqrt(2*pi*Q*S/sin(alpha)). Numeric angle 28 degrees 42 minutes equals 28.7 degrees, giving 50.15920517705 cm^2, approximately 50.16 cm^2. Q is an area and cannot be used as a radius. Included generator angle is not half the angle or a plane/base angle.
source_reviews.conditions: S,Q>0, 0<alpha<pi with a realizable right cone; in particular l^2>Q/pi and chord l*sin(alpha/2)<=r. For the supplied numbers these conditions hold.

source_reviews.independent_solution: (1) Slant l=sqrt(6^2+(10-2)^2)=10 cm. Lateral area pi*(10+2)*10=120*pi cm^2. Total area adds pi*(10^2+2^2)=104*pi, giving 224*pi cm^2. (2) tan(45 degrees)=h/(R-r), so R-r=h. With r:R=1:3, r=h/2, R=3h/2, l=h*sqrt(2). Lateral area 2*sqrt(2)*pi*h^2; both bases add (5/2)*pi*h^2. Total area pi*h^2*(2*sqrt(2)+5/2).
source_reviews.conditions: h>0; 'surface area' of the complete frustum includes both bases, unlike a lateral-only request.

source_reviews.independent_solution: The perpendicular leg is shorter than the oblique leg and is the rotation axis. The oblique leg is the frustum slant 12 cm. Its horizontal projection is 12*cos(60 degrees)=6 cm, giving radii r=2 and R=8 cm; its vertical projection is height 12*sin(60 degrees)=6*sqrt(3) cm. Lateral area pi*(2+8)*12=120*pi cm^2. Add both disks pi*(2^2+8^2)=68*pi, so total 188*pi cm^2.
source_reviews.conditions: Do not swap sine/cosine for an angle measured to the bases; the rotating solid is a frustum, not a cone or cylinder.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For any frustum, l=sqrt(h^2+(R-r)^2); developed annular-sector radii are rhoOuter=R*l/(R-r), rhoInner=r*l/(R-r), sharing angle theta=2*pi*(R-r)/l. Arc lengths are 2*pi*R and 2*pi*r. (1) R=5,r=2,h=4 gives l=5 cm, rhoOuter=25/3 cm and rhoInner=10/3 cm, theta=6*pi/5 radians=216 degrees, arcs 10*pi and 4*pi cm. (2) Diameters 28 and 20 mean radii 14 and 10 cm, h=24 gives l=4*sqrt(37) cm, developed radii 14*sqrt(37) and 10*sqrt(37) cm, theta=2*pi/sqrt(37) radians=360/sqrt(37) degrees (~59.1836), arcs 28*pi and 20*pi cm, lateral area 96*pi*sqrt(37) cm^2. If open with smaller disk as bottom, material = pi*(96*sqrt(37)+100)/10000 m^2 (~0.2148677225). If open with larger disk as bottom, replace 100 by 196 (~0.2450270120 m^2). If closed with both disks, replace 100 by 296. The current wording says bucket and two diameters but does not explicitly say which end is the bottom; the small-bottom convention is a conditional interpretation, not uniquely established numerical data.
source_reviews.conditions: No waste added. cm^2 to m^2 divides by 10000. Figure 88 depicts both bases, not a bucket-end assignment. A unique automatic material key needs explicit bottom/open-end conditions or handling of the unresolved end orientation.
